extracted.intended_audience: lawyers, criminalists, and legal fact‑finders evaluating witness testimony and expert evidence
extracted.subtask_short: evaluating witness testimony in criminal cases
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for legal practitioners (criminalists, lawyers, judges) on how to test, analyze, and infer from witness statements, expert testimony, and empirical generalizations in criminal cases. Emphasizes checking causal chains, testing expert inferences, and applying skeptical/empirical methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Investigate proximate causes and intermediary links
rubrics_metrics.description: When witnesses give long series of inferences that state only the first and last deduction, examine and investigate the intermediary links and their justification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: laymen omit proximate causes (gravity, board sprung) while professionals may specify them later; failure to examine intermediaries leads to extravagant errors that become foundation of further inference. Lawyers must test each intermediary link rather than accept only endpoints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Require explication of each step in an inference
rubrics_metrics.description: Lawyers must follow the rule of requiring explication of each step in an inference to narrow the limits of error.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Complicated deductions are valid only when each deduction has been tested; soliciting explicit steps prevents unnoticed omissions or leaps in logic. This is a practical rule to reduce mistakes from implicit assumptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not assume a unified plan or systematic motive
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid presupposing that a crime resulted from a 'moving, great, and unified plan' rather than from accident, inclination, or sudden impulse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Logical and systematic lawyers often project their own planning style onto criminals ('I would not have done this'). Consider inclination and impulsiveness as plausible causal drivers; avoid forcing a grand theoretical construction when simpler, unplanned causes fit the facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be alert to specialists' omitted correlations and leaps
rubrics_metrics.description: Professional witnesses and specialists routinely omit groups of correlations and make single‑jump conclusions about matters within their trade or area of expertise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: a hunter's testimony may skip many steps; the witness may presume the factfinder can follow his trade‑specific deductions. Counsel must call for the omitted steps and not accept professional leaps as self‑evident.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize that 'self-evident' differs between people
rubrics_metrics.description: Inferences omitted as self‑evident are a source of error because people rarely mean the same thing by 'self‑evident.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not rely on a witness's claim that something is self‑evident; ask them to articulate the basis. Professionals may imagine offhand what is not self‑evident to laypersons (example: Boltzmann's omitted steps).

rubrics_metrics.name: Test a witness's use of analogy, experience, and observation
rubrics_metrics.description: Trusting another's testimony requires being convinced they made the correct analogy, properly used experience, and observed without prejudice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The skeptic must test the witness's ability to tell the truth and to have sufficient understanding to reproduce facts correctly; examine their analogies and whether their experiences are relevant and adequate for the present inference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presume accident where causal connection is not indubitable
rubrics_metrics.description: Presuppose accident wherever a causal relationship is not indubitably and immediately excluded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two phenomena may co-occur without causal relation; the useful rule is to presuppose accident unless the causal connection is clearly demonstrated. This reduces false causal attributions from coincident occurrences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish coincidence from causation with rigorous testing
rubrics_metrics.description: Carefully examine whether observed correlations are causal or merely accidental concomitants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use examples (Tuesday rain, All-souls day coincidences) to illustrate how repeated observation can produce spurious meteorological 'laws.' Where accidental nature is not obvious, investigate exhaustively before inferring causation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Investigate early life, motive and intensity of influence
rubrics_metrics.description: Test the effect of any force or influence on an accused earlier in life; establish presence of motive or interest in the crime before judging culpability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Schopenhauer's point: recognize that small influences intensified can produce effects (bribery example). Study early life carefully; determine presence (not necessarily strength) of inclinations, passions, or motives that could reappear under proper stimulus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be skeptical of a priori claims; prefer empirical grounding
rubrics_metrics.description: Accept that all non-mathematical inferences rest on experience (Hume); treat such premises as empirical propositions rather than intellectual deductions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that presumptions and inferential knowledge depend on repeated experience. The legal factfinder must test whether the similar cases used as basis are truly similar and sufficiently numerous to justify the inference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess adequacy and representativeness of comparative examples
rubrics_metrics.description: When inferring from past cases, determine whether the examples compared are the correct ones and known in sufficiently large numbers to exclude alternatives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: traveler who never saw black people would wrongly generalize; lawyers must ask whether prior instances are exhaustive and representative before extrapolating to current case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware rules that admit no exceptions; expect exceptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Guard against accepting rules that claim no exceptions; discovery of a single exception shatters a universalizing rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical examples (black swans, monotremes, X-rays) show that 'exceptionless general rules' are rare; experts should adopt the attitude: 'we do not know if A is caused by B, but nobody has seen A without B demonstrated.' Require experts to acknowledge limits and exceptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use experiments when possible but recognize their rarity in law
rubrics_metrics.description: Where experimental replication is possible it yields more reliable causal determination, but experiments are rare in legal contexts and reliance on experience is usually necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bernard's determinism applies in natural experiments but rarely to criminal cases; when experiments cannot be done, depend on tested experience while remaining cautious about its limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat induction and analogy as risky and limited tools
rubrics_metrics.description: Induction (generalizing from instances) and analogy rest on the same foundation and are inherently hazardous for legal conclusions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lipps: if the basis for induction is doubtful the induction is unjustified. Because analogy is expressly excluded in some criminal laws, both induction and analogy should be used with caution and constant skepticism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider statistical and distributional principles only within their proper domain
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply principles like equal distribution or probabilistic expectation only when their underlying assumptions (e.g., equal possibilities) legitimately hold.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: little lottery and horse counts illustrate that probability inferences depend on domain assumptions; avoid misapplying long‑run statistical expectations to non‑random or contextually different phenomena.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not accept experts' acceptance of exceptionless norms without scrutiny
rubrics_metrics.description: Experts should not assert that phenomenon A is always caused by B without caveat; the factfinder must presume experts adopt cautious language acknowledging possible exceptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage experts to speak in qualified terms; if they do not, counsel and factfinders must presume they would have taken a more cautious attitude and scrutinize their claims accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid overgeneralizing from limited personal experience
rubrics_metrics.description: Lawyers who rely primarily on their own limited experience (even decades) risk false universalizations; seek broader, systematized evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Our profession lacks systematic inductive collections; individual practitioners must be aware that personal case experience covers only a small portion of life's possibilities and is not a reliable basis for general rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer systematic inductive procedures when positing empirical laws
rubrics_metrics.description: Empirical laws should be established by systematic induction (observation + deduction) rather than casual recollection of occurrences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jurisprudence needs more ordered collection and study of cases to make its empirical generalizations tenable; until then treat such 'laws' as provisional and subject to revision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be cautious when converting related properties to predicted behaviors
rubrics_metrics.description: When inferring that one trait implies another (e.g., maltreatment of animals → murderous inclination) apply great caution and intensive study.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conversions between related qualities (cruelty, sensuality, avarice, envy, idleness) require careful justification; these inferences are possible but difficult and demand close analysis and evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish causal/ existential nexus from mere logical nexus
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize the difference between causal/existential relations (lightning/thunder, powder/explosion) and mere conceptual connections used in deduction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lack of understanding of this distinction underlies Humian skepticism; do not confuse logical implication with real-world causal connection—always seek empirical support for causal claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Question applicability of mathematical certainty to legal facts
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not assume mathematical postulates grant certainty in human affairs; legal questions are embedded in contingent human realities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mathematical certainty is of limited relevance to jurisprudence; examples from geometry and non-Euclidean discoveries show that what seems axiom-like may be dependent on postulates. Test the postulates lawyers use.
